add.text:
Read this numbered, cleaned transcript of the owner talking. Turn it into an outline a reader
takes in at a glance: "tangible, familiar, easy to digest". The owner's words for it: "putting
familiar names, like the headings" on the thing being discussed and on each of its parts.

Output Markdown in EXACTLY this shape:

# <the concrete thing being discussed>
## <a familiar name for one part of it>
- <one point, in the owner's own words> [S#, S#]
  - <a detail or example of that point, only if it needs its own line> [S#]
## <the next part>
- <...> [S#]

Rules:
- The H1 is CONCRETE: a thing a reader could point at — a class, a page, a tab, a tool, a feature
  (the owner's example: "Page class"). Never an abstract category like "AI processes", "Thoughts"
  or "Feedback". If the transcript covers several separate things, name them plainly in the one
  H1 ("Page class and Sidebar") and give each its own H2 or H2s.
- Exactly ONE "#" H1. One "##" H2 per distinct part — never invent one just to have more.
- Each H2 is a FAMILIAR name a reader already knows. If a name already exists for that part (the
  owner's example: "Layout"), use that exact name; otherwise use the owner's own word for it.
- ONE BULLET PER POINT, NOT PER SENTENCE. When several sentences make one point (a claim, its
  reason, "so I like that"), merge them into one bullet, a short line in the owner's own words,
  citing every one of those sentences. Filler that makes no point of its own ("Couple of things.")
  gets no bullet: add its number to the nearest bullet's citation instead.
- AT MOST TWO LEVELS: a bullet, and sub-bullets under it. Never a third level.
- KEEP EVERY POINT. Merging sentences that make the same point is required; dropping a point is
  not allowed. Never turn a hedge ("maybe", "I think", "I guess") into a flat claim.
- Cite EVERY sentence number EXACTLY ONCE, in the one bullet where its main point went — never
  under two headings. Form: [S3, S7], each number individually, never a range like [S6-S9]. Use
  only numbers that appear below.

STYLE of anything the owner will read (the owner's rules):
- It is an OVERVIEW of what was said, in the owner's own key words. Never the whole rant, never a retelling.
- Each point has its answer or action baked in: say what is done, what to do, or what is still open. Do not invent an answer the transcript or the facts do not give; mark such a point open instead.
- Order by dependency and ease: clarifications and quick items first, then what depends on them. If neither applies, keep the owner's order.
- Reuse the same names for the same things every time, so they become familiar, and always name the context (the page, class, module or session) a point belongs to.
- Headings are big: "#" for the one subject, "##" for each part, "###" only when a part truly needs a split. Never "####" or smaller. Every heading starts with one fitting emoji icon.
- Under a heading: short titled lists. A status bullet starts with ✅ (done) or ⬜ (not done) when the status is known; otherwise a plain "-" bullet. Few emoji, never decoration.
- Every card cites the clean-sentence numbers it came from, like [S3, S7], each number individually.
Apply this to the headings and bullets of the outline.

Cleaned transcript:
"""
S1. Yeah, so the whole chat bubble was black, and then it all turned light gray, and I think after a pause, I think what happens is that it's using the same kind of UI indication, this change of color on the text, in order to indicate what has been sent, but the way that it goes from light gray to black, per sentence essentially, and then the whole chunk turns light gray again, and then turns black again, it's kind of like a back and forth.
S2. I'm not sure if there's a better way to do that.
S3. All right.
S4. So yeah, I need to understand the... the prompt model, yeah, so you're saying he's studying it, so the way that the prompt is...
S5. Okay, so in a normal session, prompts just go into the raw session log, and that we don't actually log every prompt, at least we haven't been.
S6. But for these voice dictations, I think it's important, and I think we don't definitely want to be logging each prompt.
S7. However, the way that that gets added to the session file, I think is important.
S8. It should be structured.
S9. Each prompt should be timestamped.
S10. The raw session, or sorry, the raw prompt should be, we don't need to save the raw whisper prompt after, before it's been cleaned, really.
S11. Unless we start getting a bunch of issues with that raw-to-clean transcription part.
S12. But generally the cleaned, the structured sentences, the list of sentences, essentially ID'd sentences, should be pretty reliable.
S13. And so then the raw prompt has, that's basically the raw prompt.
S14. That, well, it's a cleaned prompt.
S15. It's structured, but it's not necessarily refined yet in terms of organizing it and turning it into structured cards.
S16. That's what the task completion mastermind should be looking into.
S17. We need, so it's sort of independent of the chat.
S18. The chat should just be a streaming view of whatever the state of truth is those session tasks.
S19. The chat should just be a streaming view of whatever the state of truth is those session tasks.
S20. And that should go in order of when they're asked.
S21. However, doing the resurfacing thing gets a little tricky, because I do think just having the raw chat log means that I'd have to scroll up in chat to find anything.
S22. That's where the tasks tab could come in, where we could have a prioritized view of open tasks.
S23. We could then sort them by what's finished and what's not, for example.
S24. Worth working on.
S25. If the mastermind, well, you could tell it that it should resume that task when it has time.
S26. Although I don't know, the management of all these tasks is, I don't want, we need to chase down this whole prompt structure thing first.
S27. So each new prompt is...
S28. So I need to understand how the whisper data, when it's sent off for structuring and placement, essentially, I think that's the fastest system who's doing the placement, right?
S29. Let's confirm that.
S30. The way that the prompt then gets turned into the refined prompt, in terms of the data structure, in terms of the original prompt instances that are created for the, this is the, it's like a timing situation, right?
S31. When do we create a new prompt instance?
S32. When do we just add to the last one?
S33. This is sort of, well, between the fast assistant and the smart assistant, we could kind of manage the grouping of my dictations.
S34. And so, yeah, adding them to the right context card would be useful.
S35. Context cards can just be kind of temporary.
S36. They're essentially like prompt groups, but then they can get a title.
S37. And so as I'm dictating about a certain topic, those items, those prompt items can essentially get added to that specific context.
S38. But I think at the end of the day, it's really just about the tasks and questions, like, creating questions and answering them and creating tasks and finishing them.
S39. So, yeah, look at these things.
S40. Remember, I'm not reading your responses most of the time.
S41. So don't wait on me for anything.
S42. You just use the chat here for kind of updates.
S43. But yeah, that's another part of this whole system that we really need to work on.
S44. I don't want to see walls of text that I have to read and figure out what you're talking about.
S45. I want to see UI, structured UI that shows me as simply as possible, just the most important thing.
S46. If a task was completed, show me that it's checked off.
S47. And then if I want to see what it is, I can click on it and go, it needs to be interactive.
S48. That's the whole idea here is we want all of these to be as interactive as possible so that I can click through things when I want to see them and I can ignore them and scroll on when I don't.
"""

Output ONLY the Markdown described above (the H1, its H2s, and their bullets), nothing else.
